title: Pre-treatment of Seeds (Before Sowing)
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Mix one of the fungicides (Thiram, Captan, Carboxin or Carbendazim) at 2 g/kg of seed and treat the seeds at least 24 hrs prior to soaking for sprouting.

sections.heading: Dry Seed Treatment
sections.content: Mix one of the fungicides (Thiram, Captan, Carboxin or Carbendazim) at 2 g/kg of seed and treat the seeds at least 24 hrs prior to soaking for sprouting. The seeds can be stored for 30 days without any loss in viability.

title: Treatment of Seeds at the Time of Soaking for Sprouting
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Treat seeds in a solution containing Carbendazim, Pyroquilon, or Tricyclozole at 2g/lit of water for 1 kg of seed, soaking for 2 hrs, followed by sprouting and sowing in a nursery bed.

sections.heading: (a) Wet Seed Treatment
sections.content: Treat the seeds in Carbendazim or Pyroquilon or Tricyclozole solution at 2g/lit of water for 1 kg of seed. Soak the seeds in the solution for 2 hrs. Drain the solution, sprout the seeds and sow in the nursery bed. It gives protection to the seedlings up to 40 days from seedlings disease such as blast and it is better than dry seed treatment.

sections.heading: (b) Seed Treatment with Azospirillum
sections.content: Three packets (600 g/ha) of Azospirillum culture are mixed with sufficient water, wherein seeds are soaked overnight before sowing in the nursery bed. The bacterial suspension after decanting may be poured over the nursery area itself.

title: Classification
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Classification is largely based on the character of the kernels.

sections.heading: Flint Corn (Zea mays indurate)
sections.content: Starchy endosperm enclosed with hard hammy endosperm. Kernel size is large with flat bottom and round at the top, high proportion of starch, colour may be white or yellow, mostly grown in India.

sections.heading: Dent Corn (Z. mays indentata)
sections.content: Maize kernels have both soft and hard starches. The hard starch extends on the sides and the soft starch is in the centre and extends to the top of the kernel.

sections.heading: Pop Corn (Z. mays averta)
sections.content: Kernel size is small. Hard and corneous endosperm is present. After heating the pressure built up within the kernel suddenly results in an explosion of the grain is turned inside out.

sections.heading: Sweet Corn (Z. mays saccharata)
sections.content: The kernals are translucent, horny and more wrinkled when dry. Presence of recessive gene “su” (sunken-1, sunken-2) break the conversion sugar to starch in endosperm that results in sweet taste of kernels.

title: Moong Crop
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Moong is considered to be the hardiest of all pulse crops.

sections.heading: Climate and Elevation
sections.content: Moong requires a hot climate and can tolerate drought to a great extent. It can be grown from sea level to an elevation of 2000 metres.

sections.heading: Seasons
items: Rabi season crop in south and south west

sections.heading: Soil Requirements
sections.content: A well-drained loamy to sandy loam soil is best suited for moong cultivation. Saline and alkaline conditions should be avoided.

title: Varieties of Moong
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Moong varieties suitable for different seasons and regions in India.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Moong Varieties
sections.content: Moong varieties have different maturity periods, yield potentials, and resistance to diseases.

sections.heading: Variety Details
items: Samrat: matures in 60-65 days, suitable for summer and Kharif season with a yield potential of 12-15 q ha.
Pusa Vishal: matures in 65-70 days, suitable for summer and Kharif season with a yield potential of 12-15 q ha.
Asha: suitable for irrigated condition in Kharif season, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, matures in 75-80 days, and yield potential is 12-15 q ha.
Narendra moong 1: matures in 65-70 days, susceptible to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 12-15 q ha.
Pant moong 1: matures in 75 days in Kharif and 65 days in summer, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 10-12 q ha.
Pant moong 2: matures in 65-70 days in Kharif and 60-65 days in summer, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 10-12 q ha.
Pant moong 3: matures in 75-85 days and is suitable for growing in Kharif season, moderately resistant to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 10-15 q ha.
Pant moong 4: matures in 65-70 days, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 10-12 q ha.
Varsha: developed from Haryana, matures in 55-60 days, has good cooking quality, and yield potential is 10 q ha.
RS-4: developed from Rajasthan; average yield is 6-8 q ha.
Jawahar-45: suitable for eastern and western part of northern and peninsular zones of India in Kharif season, matures in 75-85 days, and yield potential is 10-13 q ha.

sections.heading: Cropping System
rows: Moong is grown as mixed crop with pigeon pea, sorghum, pearl millet, maize, and cotton during Kharif season.
Intercropping of moong can be done with spring crops.

title: Greengram and Moongbean Farming
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: Greengram and moongbean farming involves the cultivation of these two crops, which are commonly grown together in North India.

sections.heading: Field Preparation
sections.content: A thorough land levelling is must for quick drainage. The crop requires fine seedbed preparation.

sections.heading: Time of Sowing
items: Kharif: Second fortnight of June to first fortnight of July
Summer: Middle of March to middle of April

sections.heading: Seed Rate and Spacing
sections.content: During Kharif season 12-15 kg seed per hectare should be sown in 45 cm apart, while during Rabi and summer seasons 20 kg seed per hectare should be sown in rows 30 cm apart.

sections.heading: Seed Treatment
sections.content: Before sowing seed should be treated with Thiram or Carbendazim (Bavistin) at the rate of 2.5 g/kg of seed.

sections.heading: Rhizobium Culture
sections.content: Rhizobium culture is a must to get a bumper crop, as it helps in the development of nodules on the roots which are beneficial for fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil.

sections.heading: Manures and Fertilizers
sections.content: Greengram is generally raised on the residual fertility of soil. In case of light soils of poor fertility, it needs addition of organic manures like FYM or compost @ 8-10 tonnes/ha.

title: Zinc Sulphate and Elemental Sulphur for Higher Yields
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Application of 20 kg/ha each of zinc sulphate and elemental sulphur is essential for higher yields.

sections.heading: Water Management
sections.content: For rainy season crop, irrigation is not needed but drainage is very important. For Rabi and summer five to six irrigations may be given. The first irrigation should be given about 20-25 days after sowing. The subsequent irrigations should be given at an interval of 12-15 days and irrigation should be stopped after 40-45 days of sowing.

sections.heading: Weed Control
sections.content: Two weedings at 20 days interval from 25 days after sowing keep the field free from harmful weeds. Chemicals like Fluchloralin (Basalin) 1kg a.i. per hectare in 800- 1000 litres of water may be applied as pre-planting spray.

sections.heading: Diseases
sections.content: Important diseases are yellow mosaic, mosaic mottle, leaf crinkle, leaf curl, seed and seedling rot, cercospora leaf spot, anthracnose and charcoal rot. The symptoms and control measures are given below-

title: Yellow Mosaic Virus
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Symptoms of Yellow mosaic virus appear with a month of sowing, causing leaf lamina to become yellow and scattered round spots.

sections.heading: Control Measures
items: Grow resistant varieties like Asha, Pant moong-4, Narendra moong-1 etc.
Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

title: Mosaic Mottle
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Leaf margin shows upward rolling, become deformed, irregular light green areas appeared alternating with normal green in leaf surface.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Leaf margin shows upward rolling, become deformed, irregular light green areas appeared alternating with normal green in leaf surface. Control measures: Grow resistant/tolerant varieties, Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

sections.heading: Leaf Crinkle
sections.content: Symptoms appear first in third leaf after 3-4 weeks of sowing. Leaves become enlarge followed by crinkling Control measures: Rogue out disease plant as soon as they appear.

title: Leaf Curl
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A viral disease characterized by curling of leaf margins downwards, reddish-brown discoloration on the under surface of leaves, and chlorosis around lateral veins.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: It is a viral disease; chlorosis appear around the lateral vein near the leaf margin of young plants. The affected leaves show curling of margins downwards while the veins on the under surface of the leaf show reddish-brown discoloration.

sections.heading: Control Measures
items: Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

title: Cercospora Leaf Spot
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Caused by two species of cercospora fungus, small round spots with violet red in colour may be observed.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.content: Spraying of Mabcozeb 75 WP at the rate of 2 kg in 1000 litre of water per hectare at 10 days interval is very effective.

title: Anthracnose
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Diseased by fungus Colletorichum capsici, characterized by dark brown circular spot that increases in size with concentric ridges and ash color.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Diseased is caused by fungus Colletorichum capsici, dark brown circular spot appears initially, later the spots increase in size by developing concentric ridges and the colour turns into ash colour.

sections.heading: Control measures
items: Spraying of Mabcozeb 75 WP at the rate of 2 kg in 1000 litre of water per hectare at 10 days interval

title: Charcoal Rot
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Diseased is caused by a fungus Macrophomina phaseoli, characterized by rotting of roots and stems of the plant.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.content: Affected parts of the plant turn into reddish-brown to black in colour.

sections.heading: Control measures
items: 1. Diseases can be controlled by treating the seed with Brassicol (0.25%) before sowing.

title: Pod Borer
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The pod borer is a destructive insect pest that damages crops at the time of pod formation, feeding on foliage and grains within pods.

sections.heading: Characteristics
sections.content: Polyphagous in nature.

sections.heading: Damage
sections.content: Damages crops at the time of pod formation, feeding on foliage and grains within pods.

title: Hairy Caterpillar
category: Technical and Production Science | Pest Management
definition: The adult moths of these caterpillars lay eggs in large clusters and the young larvae congregated.

sections.heading: Control
sections.content: Dusting by 2% Methyl parathion dust at the rate of 25-30 kg ha can be effective to control this disease. Spraying of Endosulfan 1.5 litres in 1000 litres of water can also be efficient.

sections.heading: Control
items: Basal application of Phorate (Thimet) 10% granules at the rate of 10 kg per hectare is very effective.
Spraying of monocrotophos 36EC at the rate of ml/Litre of water can also be done.

title: Black Gram (Vigna mungo L.)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Blackgram is a pulse crop rich in protein and phosphoric acid, used for various culinary preparations and as a green manuring crop.

sections.heading: Uses of Black Gram
sections.content: It is used for preparation of 'bari' (spiced ball) which makes a delicious curry. It is the chief constituent of 'Papad.' Its husked dal is ground into a fine paste and allowed to ferment and then the fermented dal is mixed with equal quantity of rice flour to make 'dosa' and 'idli'. The dal of black gram is also used in the preparation of ‘halwa' and 'imarti'.

sections.heading: Health Benefits
sections.content: Excessive use of black gram causes flatulence which can, however be prevented by adding little as a foetida, pepper and ginger in the culinary preparations. It should not be taken by those who are easily predisposed to rheumatic diseases and urinary calculi as it contains oxalic acid in high concentration.

sections.heading: Cultivation and Uses
items: It is also an important crop for cultivating as ‘paira crop’ in paddy.
The green plant (i.e., used as fodder) is very nutritive and it is very useful to milch cow specially.

sections.heading: Environmental Benefits
rows: Black gram has deep root system which binds the soil particles very tightly
acts as cover crop and protects the soil from erosion.

title: Origin
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: Black gram is a native of India as seen from Vedic literature.

sections.heading: History
sections.content: Black gram is a native of India as is seen from Vedic literature. There is mention of urd seed in Vedic texts such as Kautilya’s “Arthasastra” and “Charak Samhita”. According to Zokovskij (1962) urd originated in India from Phaseolus sublobatus (wild progenitor).

title: Area and Distribution
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: Blackgram occupies 2.97 million ha and contributes 1.25 million tonnes to pulse production with a productivity of 419 kg/ha.

sections.heading: Regional Distribution
sections.content: The area under blackgram is highest in UP (539 ha) followed by Maharashtra (480 ha). The production under this crop is highest in Andhra Pradesh (251 tonnes) followed by UP (239 tonnes).

sections.heading: Cultivation Patterns
items: mainly as kharif crop almost in all states
in northern plains, also cultivated during spring as a catch crop
in southern and south-eastern region, cultivated in rice fallows during rabi

title: Vigna Mungo Sub-Species
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Vigna mungo is subdivided into two sub-species: Vigna mungo var. niger and Vigna mungo var. viridis.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Sub-Species
sections.content: Vigna mungo var. niger includes varieties with early maturity and black, bold seeds. Vigna mungo var. viridis includes varieties with longer maturity period, small size seeds, and green colour.

title: Climatic Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: It requires warm and humid conditions during growing season.

sections.heading: Optimum Temperature
sections.content: The optimum temperature for growth ranges from 25-35C.

sections.heading: Temperature Tolerance
sections.content: However, it can tolerate temperature up to 42C.

sections.heading: Weather Conditions
items: Heavy rains and cloudy weather at the time of germination are harmful.
Heavy rains and cloudy weather during flowering stage are harmful.

sections.heading: Day Length
sections.content: Short days are conducive for higher productivity.

title: Soil Requirement
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: Blackgram is best suited on well drained loams or slightly heavy clay loam soils with neutral pH.

sections.heading: Optimal Soil Conditions
sections.content: Well drained loams or slightly heavy clay loam soils with neutral pH are best suited.

sections.heading: Salt Tolerance and Saline Soils
sections.content: Due to its salt tolerance, it can be grown in moderate saline and alkali soils.

title: Field Preparation
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: The field should be levelled and free from weeds, with land preparation involving 1-2 deep ploughing followed by 2-3 harrowing and planking.

sections.heading: Importance of Field Preparation
sections.content: The crop does not require fine tilth but the field should be levelled and free from weeds.

sections.heading: Cropping in Rice
sections.content: Its utera cropping in rice involves no land preparation, as seeds are broadcast in standing crop of rice.

title: Sowing Time
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: The sowing time for different crop seasons varies depending on the climatic condition.

sections.heading: Seasonal Sowing Times
sections.content:
The sowing time for different crop seasons are:

(i)Kharif: Onset of monsoon in later part of June and early part of July.
(ii)Rabi: October to November.
(iii) Pre-Kharif or zaid : Last week of February to first week of April.

title: Seed Rate and Spacing
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The seed rate and spacing of a crop vary depending on the season, with different rates required for kharif, other seasons, and utera cropping.

sections.heading: General Guidelines
sections.content: In kharif, the crop is sown in rows 30-45 cm apart due to vigorous plant growth, while in other seasons, a narrow row of 20-30 cm is recommended. The plants are thinned to a spacing of 5-10 cm after germination and establishment.

sections.heading: Seed Rate
items: Double the seed rate of kharif for other seasons

sections.heading: Optimum Population and Seeding Depth
sections.content: The optimum population is 4 lakh/ha in kharif, and 10 lakh/ha in spring and summer seasons. The optimum seeding depth is 4-6 cm.

title: Seed Treatment
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Seed should be treated with specific chemicals or microorganisms before sowing to prevent disease incidence.

sections.heading: Chemical Seed Treatments
sections.content: Seed should be treated with Agrosan GN or Emison-6 or Carbendazim 50% (Bavistin) or Mancozeb 75% WP (Dithane M-45, Indofil M-45 etc.) @ 3.0 g or Trichoderma viridi @ 5 g per kg of seed before sowing to prevent the incidence of diseases.

sections.heading: Microbial Seed Inoculation
sections.content: Seed should be inoculated with Rhizobium culture for better nodulation and nitrogen fixation.

title: Cropping System with Black Gram
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Black gram can be grown in various cropping systems, including rotations with other crops like rice, potato, maize, sorghum, wheat, pigeon pea, mustard, mungbean, and as an intercrop with sugarcane and sorghum.

sections.heading: Importance of Black Gram Cropping Systems
sections.content: Black gram can be grown in various cropping systems, including rotations with other crops like rice, potato, maize, sorghum, wheat, pigeon pea, mustard, mungbean, and as an intercrop with sugarcane and sorghum.

sections.heading: Mixed/ Intercropping of Black Gram
sections.content: Black gram can be grown mixed with other traditional crops like sorghum, maize, pearlmillet, pigeonpea during Kharif Season.

title: Black Gram
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Black gram has a slow growth during its first 75-90 days.

sections.heading: Benefits of Black Gram
sections.content: This space could otherwise be occupied by weeds causing some problem to crop. In case of paired row planting, two rows are made closer and thus this extra space is provided in between two pairs of rows.

sections.heading: Inter Cropping with Sugarcane
items: Black gram may be inter cropped with spring planted Sugarcane.

title: Varieties of Crops
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A variety is a specific type or cultivar of a plant species, distinguished by its unique characteristics.

sections.heading: B-76 (Kalindi)
sections.content: Plant is dwarf and bushy. Pods are hairy and seed are bold and black in colour. Mature in 80-85 days with yield 15-20 q/ha. This variety is suitable for sowing from end of February to early July in West Bengal.

sections.heading: HPU-6
sections.content: Mature in 100-120 days with yield of 10-12 q/ha. It is a suitable variety for growing in Kangra and Kulu Valleys of Himachal Pradesh.

sections.heading: Krishna
sections.content: The variety gives average yield of 8-10 q/ha in 90-100 days maturity period. Seed are bold and black in colour.

sections.heading: Kulu-4
sections.content: Maturity period is 120 days. Average yield is 8-10 q/ha. It is a suitable variety for cultivation in Kulu Valley in Himacba1pradesh.

sections.heading: Mash-48
sections.content: It is a semi dwarf variety with average yield of 15-20 q/ha. It is resistant to drought. Plants are spreading type. Maturity day is 85-90 days. It is susceptible to viral disease.

sections.heading: Naveen
sections.content: Maturity period is 90-95 days. Seed are yellowish green in colour. Average yield is 10-12 q/ha. It is a suitable variety for cultivation in North Bihar as a catch crop between harvesting of maize and sowing of wheat.

sections.heading: Pant U-19
sections.content: Plant are erect and short with maturity period of 80-85 days in Kharif and 75 days in spring and summer. Pods are hairy and black at maturity. Average yield is 10-12 q/ha. It is resistant to yellow mosaic virus disease.

sections.heading: Pant U-30
sections.content: Plant identified: Short and erect. Pod: Hairy and black at maturity: Seed: Medium in size and brown in colour. Maturity: 80-85 days. It is resistant to powdery mildew and yellow mosaic disease. Yield: 12-15 q/ha.

sections.heading: Pusa-I
sections.content: Plants are medium tall and semi spreading with average yield of 12-15 q/ha. Pods are medium long and hairy containing 5-6 seeds. It is resistant to yellow mosaic disease.

sections.heading: T-9
sections.content: Plants are dwarf and semi-erect with dark green leaves and hairy pods. Average yield is 10-12.5 q/ha. This variety is susceptible to yellow mosaic disease. It is suitable for cultivation for summer and spring season. This variety is recommended for general cultivation in Haryana. It is a short duration (75-90 days) variety.

title: Fertilizer Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Apply 20 kg nitrogen with 40-60 kg PO/ha.

sections.heading: Seed Treatment
sections.content: Seed treatment with rhizobium helps in better nitrogen fixation. Seed treatment with PSB improves phosphorous availability to the plants.

sections.heading: Fertilizer Application
items: Drill fertilizers 5-7 cm below seed at sowing time.
Application of S @ 20 kg/ha and Mo 0.5 kg/ha is beneficial.

sections.heading: Inter cropping
sections.content: Fertilizer applied to main crop may also meet its requirement when raised as intercrop.

title: Water Management in Black Gram
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Irrigation in black gram depends upon the amount and distribution of rainfall during the growing season.

sections.heading: Requirements for Irrigation
sections.content: In the absence of rains, irrigation should be given at flowering and pod filling stage.

sections.heading: Irrigation Schedules
items: Under irrigated conditions of rabi, spring and summer seasons

title: Weed Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The management of weeds in agricultural settings is crucial to ensure crop health and productivity.

sections.heading: Importance of Weed Control
sections.content: The short stature of crop in sole stands provides scope for intense weed competition. Initial 30-40 days after sowing is critical period of crop-weed competition.

sections.heading: Recommended Weed Control Methods
items: Two hand weeding at 20-25 and 30-40 days after sowing
Pre-plant incorporation of fluchloralin or pre-emergence application of pendimethalin or alachlor @ 1 kg/ha

title: Disease Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Disease management
definition: Spraying the crop with specific chemicals at certain concentrations can help manage diseases.

sections.heading: Cercospora Leaf Scope
sections.content: Angular, brown or red colour spots with grey or brown centre and radish purple border are formed on leaves, stalks and pods.

sections.heading: Treatment for Cercospora Leaf Scope
items: Spray the crop with Blitox -50 or Indofil M -45 @ 1.5 to 2.0 Kg/ha in 500 l of water.

sections.heading: Bacterial Leaf Scope
sections.content: Symptoms appear as water soaked dots on the under surface of the leaf which remain small in size and the surrounding tissues becomes necrotic.

sections.heading: Treatment for Bacterial Leaf Scope
items: Spray the crop with copper oxychloride @ 1.52 to 2.0 Kg in 500 l of water.

title: Root Rot
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Affected plants show yellow and green areas on leaves, badly affected leaves turn completely yellow, and reduce yields considerably.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.content: To control this disease, treat the seed with thiram @4 g/kg seed.

title: Pigeonpea (Cajanus cajan L.)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Pigeonpea is the second most important pulse crop in the country.

sections.heading: Uses of Pigeonpea
sections.content: It is consumed extensively as dal, as it is rich in protein (21%), iron and iodine. It is also rich in essential amino acids like lycine, tyrocene, cystine and arginine.

sections.heading: Other Uses of Pigeonpea
items: The pod husk and seed husk are used as feed for cattle.
The dry sticks are used for thatching and fuel purpose.

sections.heading: Environmental Benefits of Pigeonpea
sections.content: Pigeonpea being a legume possesses valuable property as restorer of nitrogen in soil. The plants shed large number of leaves, which add organic matter to soil.

title: Origin of Pigeonpea
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: India is believed to be the center of origin and diversity of pigeonpea.

sections.heading: Geographical Distribution
sections.content: The closest wild relative of pigeonpea (Atylosia canifolia) was found in India and Australia. The centre of origin is the eastern part of peninsular India, including the state of Orissa, where the closest wild relatives (Cajanus cajanifolia) occur in tropical deciduous woodlands.

sections.heading: Domestication
sections.content: From India it was domesticated to East Africa and West Africa. There was first encountered by Europeans, so it obtained the name Congo Pea. By means of the slave trade, it came to the American continent, probably in the 17th century.

title: Pigeonpea Area and Distribution
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Pigeonpea is grown in over 50 tropical countries, mainly in Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

sections.heading: Major Regions of Cultivation
sections.content: Pigeonpea is mainly grown in Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

sections.heading: Early-Maturing Varieties
sections.content: In Punjab and Haryana, early-maturing varieties are grown, which escape frost.

title: Cajanus indicus
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A type of legume that comprises two varieties: Cajanus indicus var. bicolor (arhar) and Cajanus indicus var. flavus (tur).

sections.heading: Characteristics of Cajanus indicus var. bicolor (Arhar)
sections.content: Late-maturing, tall and bushy perennial types with dark coloured pods containing 4 to 5 seeds.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Cajanus indicus var. flavus (Tur)
sections.content: Early maturing, relatively short stature varieties with yellow flowers and plain pods containing 2-3 seeds.

title: Climatic Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Pigeonpea can be grown in a wide range of climatic conditions, including tropical and subtropical areas with temperatures between 20°-40°C.

sections.heading: Optimum Conditions
sections.content: Moist and humid conditions during the vegetative phase and dry conditions during the reproductive phase are suitable for successful raising of pigeonpea.

sections.heading: Photoperiod and Light Intensity
sections.content: Pigeonpea is a short-day plant with a critical photoperiod of 13 hours. Low light intensity at pod formation is harmful.

title: Soil Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Pigeonpea can be grown on a wide range of soils, but sandy loam to clay loams are ideal.

sections.heading: Ideal Soil Conditions
sections.content: The soil should be deep, well drained and free from soluble salts.

sections.heading: Limitations Due to Soil Acidity
sections.content: It cannot tolerate soil acidity owing to aluminium toxicity.

title: Cropping System
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Pigeonpea can be intercropped or sown mixed with a number of other crops, such as sorghum, maize, rice, groundnut, sesame, urdbean, greengram, cowpea, ragi and soybean, and an additional yield may be obtained.

sections.heading: Cropping System Details
sections.content: There is a possibility of raising early maturing pigeonpea as a summer crop with intercrop of greengram or cowpea. In this cropping system, pigeonpea may be sown in mid-April keeping a row-to-row distance of 75-90 cm, intercropped with 2-3 rows of greengram.

sections.heading: Harvest Timing
sections.content: Greengram becomes ready for harvest by the end of June (65-70 DAS).

title: Field Preparation
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: A clod and weed-free seed-bed for proper germination and establishment of seedlings is achieved by opening the soil through soil-turning plough or disc harrow followed by the cross-harrowing or ploughing with desi plough on or before the onset of monsoon.

sections.heading: Importance of Field Preparation
sections.content: Thorough levelling is essential for quick drainage and also to avoid water logging. Sowing pigeonpea on a ridge and furrow planting is preferred to overcome water logging.

title: Sowing Method
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Seed should be sown behind the plough or with the help of seed drill in rows.

sections.heading: Row Spacing
sections.content: The row spacing in kharif varies from 40-60 cm in short and medium duration varieties to 60-90 cm in long duration varieties. In rabi season, the crop is grown in 30 cm rows.

sections.heading: Thinning
sections.content: After germination, the seedlings are thinned to maintain an intra-row spacing of 15-20 cm.

title: Seed Treatment
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Seed should be treated with thiram @ 2.5 g/kg seed, Rhizobium culture, or Trichoderma harzianum before sowing.

sections.heading: Inoculation Methods
sections.content: Seed inoculation with Trichoderma harzianum alone or serial inoculation of T. harzianum, followed by Rhizobium may significantly reduce wilt incidence, enhance nodulation and root/shoot growth.

title: Sowing Pigeonpea
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The sowing time for pigeonpea should be adjusted to avoid rains and frost at flowering and reproductive stages.

sections.heading: Regional Sowing Times
sections.content: For early rabi planting in Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, September sowing is ideal. The rabi cultivation of pigeonpea in rice fallows is increasingly popular, and is sown immediately after rice harvest in southern India.

sections.heading: Specific Sowing Times by Region
items: Uttar Pradesh and northern Rajasthan: mid of June to July end, second fortnight of June
Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal: September
Southern India: immediately after rice harvest
First fortnight of April for double cropping (medium-early varieties)

sections.heading: Late Pigeonpea Sowing
sections.content: The late pigeonpea is sown with the onset of monsoon, preferably by first week of July.

title: Fertilizer Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The recommended fertilizer dose is 15-20 kg N and 40-60 kg PO/ha.

sections.heading: Seed Treatment
sections.content: Seed treatment with Rhizobium culture is beneficial.

sections.heading: Convenient Application
sections.content: 100 kg diammonium phosphate is applied per hectare area.

sections.heading: PSB Culture
sections.content: Use of PSB culture improves the available phosphorus status in the soil.

title: Water Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Long duration pigeonpea with deep root system can withstand drought, while short duration cultivars require irrigation.

sections.heading: Importance of Irrigation
sections.content: The critical stages for irrigation are branching, flowering and pod filling.

sections.heading: Water Requirements
items: 20-25 cm water to produce a tonne of grain.

sections.heading: Irrigation at Critical Stages
sections.content: At times of prolonged drought, irrigation at flowering and pod filling stages is highly rewarding in Kharif.

title: Weed Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Keeping crops free from weeds during critical periods is important for weed control.

sections.heading: Critical Periods of Weed Competition
sections.content: The initial 7-8 weeks period of crop sowing to branching stage is critical, while in short duration varieties it is the first 4-6 weeks.

sections.heading: Weed Control Methods
rows: Hand-weeding at 25 and 45 days after sowing
Application of weedicide immediately after sowing

title: Disease Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Disease management
definition: Control measures for various plant diseases include treating seeds with thiram, using resistant varieties, crop rotation, removing excess water, and ensuring proper aeration.

sections.heading: Causes of Diseases
sections.content: Various plant diseases are caused by viruses, mites, and fungi.

sections.heading: Types of Diseases
items: Wilt: The plant remains green and show wilting. Removal of roots shows browning of the xylum which curtail the uptake of nutrients.
Sterility mosaic: This is caused by virus. The virus is transmitted by mites which results in malformation of flowers and no pods will be formed.
Phytophthora stem blight: Brown colour spots will appear on the stem and the rotting will start at these spots and plant becomes week and fall down.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.content: Before sowing, seed should be treated with thiram @ 2.5 g/kg seed. Use of resistant varieties is best in disease-prone areas. Use crop rotation. Remove the excess rain or irrigation water. There should be proper aeration in the field.

title: Insect Management: Pod Borer
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Pod borer is the major insect in North India.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.content: For its control, spray monocrotophos 36 SL@750 ml/ha or 187.5 ml cypermethrin 25 EC or 300 ml fenvalerate 20 EC or 537.5 ml deltamethrin 2.8 EC in 750 liters of water per hactare at 50 % pod formation stage.

title: Threshing and Drying Seeds
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The process of separating seeds from their pods, typically involving threshing, winnowing, and drying to achieve a suitable moisture content.

sections.heading: Threshing
sections.content: Ground and bundled. These are taken to threshing floor and staked upright, dried for a few days and shaken vigorously to separate pods.

sections.heading: Winnowing
sections.content: The resultant material, i.e. pods and dry leaves, is beaten with sticks or is trampled by bullocks. The seeds and husk are separated by winnowing.

sections.heading: Drying
sections.content: Threshed and cleaned produce should be further sun dried to reduce the moisture content to 10-11%.

title: Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea L.)
category: Technical and Production Science | Legumes
definition: The groundnut is a legume crop that belongs to the family Leguminosae/Fabaceae, resistant to soil erosion and useful as a rotational crop.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Groundnuts
sections.content: Groundnut cake is chief oil cake feed to animals (7-8% N, 1.5% P2O5 and 1.2% K2O) and also used as manure.

sections.heading: Nutritional Value of Groundnuts
items: rich in nutrients, providing over 30 essential nutrients and phytonutrients
good source of niacin, folate, fiber, magnesium, vitamin E, manganese and phosphorus

title: Origin and History of Groundnut
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Groundnut is a native of Brazil, South America.

sections.heading: History of Spread
sections.content: The crop has spread from Brazil to Peru, Argentina and Ghana, from where it was introduced by the Portuguese into Africa from where it was introduced into Jamaica, Cuba, West Indies islands and North America.

sections.heading: Global Expansion
items: from Mexico across the Pacific to Philippines
then spread to China, India, Malaysia and Indonesia

title: Area and Distribution
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Groundnut is grown in almost all tropical and subtropical countries of the world.

sections.heading: Productivity by State
sections.content: Tamil Nadu has the highest productivity (1630 kg ha), followed by Gujarat (1360 kg ha).

title: Groundnuts
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Groundnuts have been divided into two groups: the erect or bunch type and the trailing or spreading type.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Groundnut Types
sections.content: Morphologically groundnuts have been divided into two groups. The erect or bunch type-include Arachis hypogaea subspecies fastigiata. Pods in erect type are borne in bunch close to the base of plant. Erect types are normally short duration. Seeds have no dormancy and sometimes the first form pod may sprout before harvest if conditions are suitable. This is due to presence of water-soluble auxins.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Groundnut Types
items: The trailing or spreading type-include Arachis hypogaea subspecies procumbens.
Pods are spreading so harvesting is difficult. Comparatively it is longer duration crop than bunch type.

title: Climatic Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Groundnut is grown in the tropics and subtropical countries, lying between 45ºN and 35ºS, and up to an altitude of 1000 m.

sections.heading: Ideal Climate Conditions
sections.content: The arid and semi-arid regions with 500-700 mm rainfall during crop growth period are ideal for ground production. The crop can be grown successfully in places receiving a maximum rainfall of 1250 mm.

sections.heading: Climate Limitations
sections.content: The groundnut, however, cannot withstand frost, long and severe drought or water stagnation.

sections.heading: Soil Temperature Requirements
sections.content: It seems that plant will grow best when the mean temperature is from 24-33ºC. During ripening period, it requires about a month of warm and dry weather.

title: Soil Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Groundnut thrives best in well-drained sandy and sandy loam soils, with pH between 6.0-6.5.

sections.heading: Optimal Soil Conditions
sections.content: Groundnut is grown on a wide variety of soil types but, thrives best in well-drained sandy and sandy loam soils, as light soil helps in easy penetration of pegs. Heavy and stiff clays are not desirable for groundnut cultivation as pod development is hampered in those soils.

sections.heading: Soil pH
sections.content: Groundnut gives good yields in the soils with pH between 6.0-6.5.

title: Cropping Systems
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Groundnut is grown in rotation with various crops, including wheat, lentil, chickpea, pea, barley, pearl millet, maize, sorghum, castor, cotton, and safflower.

sections.heading: Common Cropping Systems
sections.content: The most common cropping systems are: Groundnut-wheat/barley/ chickpea/field pea / lentil.

sections.heading: Regional Variations
items: Sorghum is grown after harvest of groundnut in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra.

title: Field Preparation
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Deep ploughing should be avoided for groundnut due to difficulties in harvesting, but a combination of soil turning plough followed by two harrowings can achieve good surface tilth up to 12-18 cm depth.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.content: Deep ploughing should be avoided for groundnut due to difficulties in harvesting, but a combination of soil turning plough followed by two harrowings can achieve good surface tilth up to 12-18 cm depth.

title: Seed Treatment
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Seeds should be shelled by hand one week before sowing to prevent damage, and treated with a fungicide to check for diseases.

sections.heading: Preparation of Seeds
sections.content: Pods should be shelled by hand one week before sowing. Hand shelling ensures little damage to seeds. Pods shelled long before sowing time are liable to suffer from loss of viability and storage damages.

sections.heading: Seed Treatment with Fungicides
sections.content: Treat the selected kernels with 5 g of Thiram or Captan or Ceresan per kg of kernels so as to check various seed and soil borne diseases.

sections.heading: Inoculation with Rhizobium Culture
sections.content: Seed should be inoculated with proper strain of Rhizobium culture particularly in those places where groundnut is to be grown for the first time.

title: Seed Rate, Spacing and Sowing Method
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Seed rate depends upon the growth habit of variety and seed weight for obtaining good yields.

sections.heading: General Guidelines
sections.content: Seed rate can vary according to the region also. In bunch types, the row-to-row distance is kept 30-40 cm and in spreading types 45-60 cm.

sections.heading: Seeding Requirements
items: 80-100 kg of seeds per hectare for bunch types

sections.heading: Plant-to-Plant Distance
sections.content: Plant to plant distance would be 15 and 20-22.5 cm for bunch and spreading types respectively.

sections.heading: Sowing Depth
sections.content: The depth of sowing should be 5 cm.

title: Fertilizer Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Groundnut needs more phosphorous, sulphur, calcium, and nitrogen for its growth.

sections.heading: Nutrient Requirements
sections.content: Groundnut needs more phosphorous, sulphur, calcium, and nitrogen for its growth.

items: can be partially met by seed inoculation with efficient strains of rhizobium

title: Maintaining Organic Carbon in Soil for Good Yields
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: A desirable level of organic carbon in the soil (0.3-0.7%) must be maintained to ensure overall health of soil and continued good yields.

sections.heading: Fertilizer Application
sections.content: Apply 15 kg N, 50 kg P2O5 and 25 kg ZnSO4/ha at the time of sowing. Phosphorus should be applied preferably through single super phosphate; it provides sulphur in addition to phosphorous.

sections.heading: Fertilizer Placement
sections.content: The fertilizers should be placed at the time of sowing about 4-5 cm in the side of the seed and 4-5 cm below the seed level.

sections.heading: Calcium and Yield
sections.content: Calcium too has pronounced effect on proper development of pods and kernels. Use of gypsum @ 100-150 kg/ha at the time of field preparation can add to the yield.

title: Water Management for Groundnuts
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Groundnut does not require irrigation as a rainy season crop, but care should be taken to ensure the soil is friable and has sufficient moisture content.

sections.heading: Importance of Irrigation in Groundnut Cultivation
sections.content: Irrigations are necessary in southern part of country where groundnut grown in Rabi season too, three to four irrigations are necessary.

sections.heading: Last Irrigation Before Harvesting
sections.content: The last irrigation before harvesting will facilitate the full recovery of pods from the soil.

title: Scheduling of Irrigation
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Irrigation at 25% depletion of available soil moisture throughout the growth period results in high pod yield.

sections.heading: Optimal Irrigation Schedules
sections.content: Irrigation at 25% depletion of available soil moisture from pegging to early pod development and at 50% DASM at other stages appears to be ideal for high water use efficiency.

sections.heading: IW/CPE Ratio for High Water Use Efficiency
sections.content: An IW/CPE ratio of 1.0 at moisture sensitive stages and 0.6 during other stages leads to high water use efficiency.

title: Weed Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A reduction of 20-45% in yield due to weeds has been recorded.

sections.heading: Recommended Weed Control Measures
sections.content: Two weedings 20 and 45 (days after sowing) DAS are recommended. No weeding or intercultural operation should be done after pegging has commenced; pegs have started moving undergrounds.

sections.heading: Earthing Up
sections.content: Earthing up can be done in bunch and semi spreading types to facilitate maximum penetration of pegs.

sections.heading: Pre-Emergence Application
items: Pre- emergence application of Pendimethalin @ 1 kg a.i./ha along with 2 inter-cultures at 30 and 45 DAS have been recommended in irrigated conditions.
Fluchloralin (Basalin) at the rate of 1 kg a.i. per hectare dissolved in 800-1000 litres of water can also be used as pre-planting incorporation.

title: Disease Management
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The management of diseases in groundnut crops.

sections.heading: Tikka Disease or Leaf Spot
sections.content: Cercospora arachidicola and Cercospora personatum cause Tikka disease, appearing 3-4 weeks after sowing. Spots on leaves are circular to irregular, surrounded by a yellow halo, and can be reddish brown to black on the upper surface and smooth and light brown on the lower surface.

sections.heading: Collar Rot and Seed Rot
sections.content: Aspergillus niger causes collar rot and seed rot. Symptoms include rotting of seeds, soft rot of hypocotyls, and post emergence collar rot of seedlings. Treatment involves using Thiram or Captan on healthy seeds.

sections.heading: Sclerotium Rot
sections.content: Sclerotium rolfsii causes sclerotium rot, characterized by white thread-like fungal growth and yellow to brown leaves. Soil application of Brassicol before sowing is beneficial.

sections.heading: Charcoal Rot
sections.content: Microphomina phaseoli causes charcoal rot, marked by a red-brown water-soaked lesion on the stem of infected plants. Spraying Brassicol before sowing is effective.

sections.heading: Rust
sections.content: Puccinia arachidis causes rust, characterized by red pustules on leaves that turn dark brown. Treatment involves spraying Zineb as soon as symptoms appear.

title: Insect Management: White Grub
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: White-grub, a menace in the light soils of Rajasthan, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana can be controlled effectively by treating seed with Chlorpyriphos 20 EC or Quinalphos 25 EC@ 15 ml/kg of seeds.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.content: White grubs live in soil and remain active from July

title: Pest Control in Agriculture
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Controlling pests such as aphids, jassids, thrips, moths, and leaf minor using various methods including spraying pesticides.

sections.heading: Pest Control Methods
sections.content: Using light traps to destroy moths may control leaf minor. Carbaryl 50 WP 0.02% spray is most economical.

sections.heading: Spraying Pesticides
items: Spray 500 ml malathion 50EC in 500 lt. of water per hectare

title: Aflatoxin
category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
definition: A carcinogenic substance produced by mould such as Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus in kernels during post harvest processing and storage.

sections.heading: Prevention and Control Measures
sections.content: It is desirable to store groundnuts in gunny bags as pods rather than kernels. The gunny bags are stacked in a store-room over planks in tiers comprising not more than ten in each in such a way that air keeps circulating.

sections.heading: Detoxification Methods
items: Exposure to sunlight for an hour (removes nearly 90% of aflatoxin)
Chemicals such as chloride, peroxide, sodium bisulphate

title: Soybean (Glycine max L. Merril)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Soybean is an important pulse crop rich in food value.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Uses of Soybean
sections.content: It is a cheapest, richest and easiest source of best quality protein and fat. It is more considered as oilseed crop owing to its multiplicity of uses as food and industrial products, it is called a ‘wonder crop or miracle crop’. It is the number one oilseed crop of the world which contains 40% protein and 20% oil.

sections.heading: Nutritional Value of Soybean
sections.content: Soybean protein is rich in the valuable amino acid lysines (5%) in which most of the cereals are deficient. The seeds contain good quality protein rich in lysine and oil is having considerable amount of essential fatty acids (Omega-6 and Omega-3). It also contains phytochemicals known as isoflvines which protect human body against chronic diseases such as cancer, diabetes, osteoporosis and blood pressure.

sections.heading: Benefits of Soybean for Soil Fertility
sections.content: Soybean, being leguminous crop, improves the soil fertility by fixing atmospheric nitrogen and also through leaf fall at maturity.

sections.heading: Animal Feed Uses of Soybean
rows: excellent nutritive foods for livestock and poultry
excellent nutritive foods for livestock and poultry

sections.heading: History of Soybean Origin
sections.content: The wild ancestor of the soybean is Glycine soja (previously called G. ussuriensis), a slender twining vine legume native to central China and Korea.

sections.heading: Introduction to India

title: Climatic Requirement for Soybean
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Soybean grows well in warm and moist climates from sea level to an elevation of 3,000 m.

sections.heading: Optimum Temperature Range
sections.content: The optimum temperature range for germination is 15-32C, while the optimal temperature range for growth and development is 26.5-30C.

sections.heading: Temperature Effects on Oil Content
items: Higher temperatures during seed formation increase oil content in seed.

sections.heading: Temperature and Nodulation
sections.content: Temperatures above 42C severely hamper nodulation, while temperatures below 18C prevent pod setting.

sections.heading: Optimum Relative Humidity for Pod Formation
sections.content: A relative humidity of 70-75% is optimum for pod formation.

sections.heading: Tolerance to Frost and Water Logging
sections.content: Soybean cannot tolerate frost and water logging.

sections.heading: Growth Requirements
items: A photoperiod of 13-14 hours, provided that temperatures are favourable.

sections.heading: Characteristics

In southern part of the country, soybean has a good scope as intercrop in cotton, sorghum, pigeonpea, groundnut and sugarcane. In central India, it has been found very remunerative on the fallow lands in Kharif.

sections.heading: Sowing Seasons

title: Field Preparation
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: The seed bed should be well pulverized, free from clods and perennial weeds, and well leveled.

sections.heading: Steps for Field Preparation
sections.content: The land should be prepared by ploughing 4-5 times followed by planking after each ploughing. Generally one deep ploughing with mould board plough followed by 3-4 light ploughings by desi plough will ensure the proper tilth.

title: Seed Rate
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The amount of seed required per hectare for a specific crop or crop combination.

sections.heading: General Seed Rates
sections.content: Soybean crop needs about 70-80 kg/ha seed during kharif season (timely sown) and 100-120 kg/ha seed during spring and summer seasons (late sown). Intercropping with other crops either in alternate rows or 2 rows of soybean between two rows of main crop would require 60% of the seed rate.

sections.heading: Seed Rate Variations Based on Crop Variety
items: Small seeded varieties require 55-60 kg/ha seed.
Medium and bold seeded varieties require 70-75 kg/ha and 80-90 Kg/ha, respectively.

title: Sowing Method
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The seeds are sown by different methods, including seed drill or behind the plough.

sections.heading: General Guidelines for Sowing Soybean
sections.content: Soybean can be planted at spacing of 45 cm row to row and 4-5 cm plant to plant. A seeding depth of 5 cm is optimum.

sections.heading: Effects of Rainfall on Sowing
sections.content: Rainfall immediately after sowing results in crust formation inhibiting seedling emergence.

sections.heading: Soybean as an Inter Crop
items: pigeonpea, cotton and upland paddy in northern India
sorghum, cotton, sugarcane, pigeonpea and groundnut in southern India

sections.heading: Paired Row Method
sections.content: The paired row method utilizes the resources more efficiently with higher yield.

title: Seed Treatment
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Seeds must be treated with Thiram or Captan @ 2g/kg seed or Trichoderma viridi @ 5 gm. per kg of seed to get rid of seed borne diseases.

sections.heading: Importance of Seed Treatment
sections.content: The inoculation of seed with Rhizobium culture is most important when the crop is cultivated first time in any land.

sections.heading: Rhizobium Culture for Soybean
sections.content: Seeds should be inoculated with Rhizobium japonicum strains of soybean culture to overcome the problem of poor nodulation.

sections.heading: Storage and Sowing of Inoculated Seeds
sections.content: Inoculated seeds are stored under shade till the time of sowing. Sowing should be finished within two hours of inoculation.

title: Fertilizer Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A fertilizer requirement refers to the amount of nutrients needed by a crop for growth.

sections.heading: Nitrogen Requirements
sections.content: An application of 25 kg N/ha as a starter dose will be sufficient to meet the nitrogen requirement of the crop in initial stage. A response of higher nitrogen application has been observed in fields deficient in nitrogen.

sections.heading: Phosphorus and Potassium Requirements
sections.content: Apply 80 kg PO/ha to meet the phosphorous demand of the crop at the time of sowing. In K deficient soils, basal application of 40 kg KO/ha is recommended.

sections.heading: Sulfur Requirements
sections.content: In areas with low S availability, 20 kg S/ha is necessary.

sections.heading: Zinc Requirements
sections.content: Application of 20 kg ZnSO /ha recommendation is made for all soybean growing zones.

title: Water Management
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: Irrigation at active growth stage is required; however there should not be any moisture stress at the end of flowering to pod initiation stages.

sections.heading: Requirements for Irrigation
sections.content: The crop requires about 600-650 mm rainfall. Soil deficient in moisture requires pre-sowing irrigation for the good germination. Irrigation at active growth stage is required; however there should not be any moisture stress at the end of flowering to pod initiation stages. In rainfed crop prolonged dry spells, requires protective irrigation .The spring or summer crop of soybean requires assured irrigation facilities.

sections.heading: Importance of Timing
sections.content: Irrigation at active growth stage is required; however there should not be any moisture stress at the end of flowering to pod initiation stages.

title: Weed Management

definition: To avoid weed competition during initial stage, soybean field should be kept weed free for the first 30-40 days after sowing.

sections.heading: Weeding Methods

sections.heading: Pre-Plant Incorporation and Pre-Emergence Application
items: pre-emergence application of pendimethalin @ 1 kg/ha or metribuzin @ 0.75 kg/ha

sections.heading: Post-Emergence Herbicides

title: Disease Management - Bacterial Blight
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Bacterial blight is characterized by small reddish-brown spots surrounded by water-soaked margins with yellow holes on pods, often appearing in cool and moist conditions.

sections.heading: Causes and Conditions
sections.content: Cool and moist conditions are favourable for bacterial blight.

sections.heading: Symptoms
items: Small reddish-brown spot surrounded by water-soaked margin with yellow holes on pods
Yellow pustules appear on leaves which later changes to reddish brown with marginal yellowing

title: Bacterial Pustules
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Conditions favourable for bacterial pustules can be controlled by using disease-free seed, practicing crop rotation, and growing resistant variety.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.content: The seed should be treated with Cerasan or Captan @ 3.0 g per kg of seed or Trichoderma viridi @ 5 gm per kg of seed before sowing. The crop should be sprayed twice with Copper Oxychloride 50 % WP (Blitox) or Streptocycline (500 ppm) at an interval of 10 days depending on the severity of the disease.

sections.heading: Downy Mildew (Pernospora Sp)
sections.content: Small chlorotic spots appear on the upper surface of the leaves which later turn greyish to dark brown with downy growth on the lower surface of the leaves. For control, the seed should be treated with Captan @ 3.0 gm per kg of seed before sowing.

sections.heading: Dry Root Rot (Macrophomina phaseoli (Tassi) Goid)
sections.content: Small, round or irregular black sclerotia appears below the epidermis on the affected stem and root. The plant wilts within a week. On examination of the stem, dark sunken lesions are seen on the stem and dry rot symptoms appear on basal stem and main root.

sections.heading: Yellow Mosaic (Virus)
sections.content: The affected leaves become yellow with a slight crinkling and reduction in size. The plants are stunted in growth and set a few pod only. Regular spraying of the crop with a mixture of Methyl demiton 25 EC (Metasystox 25 EC) @ 1.5 ml per litre of water starting from third week or onwards at an interval of 10-15 days keep the white fly population under control and the crop becomes free from the incidence of yellow mosaic virus.

title: Sesame (Sesamum indicum L.)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Sesame is a member of the family Pedaliaceae, comprising sixteen genera and about sixty species, several of which can be crossed with S. indicum.

sections.heading: Origin
sections.content: The origin of cultivated sesame (Sesamum indicum L.) is generally accepted as the Ethiopian area in Africa, with considerable argument in favour of Afghan-Persian region or even a polytopic origin.

sections.heading: Genome Grouping
sections.content: The genus sesame can be grouped into three on the basis of chromosome number: Group I (2n=26), Group II (2n=32), and Group III (2n=64).

sections.heading: Climatic Requirement
sections.content: Sesame is considered a crop of the tropics and subtropics, but its cultivation can be extended to the temperate zone by breeding suitable varieties.

title: Sesame Cultivation
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Sesame is a crop that requires hot conditions for high yield, with optimal temperatures between 25-27 C.

sections.heading: Optimal Temperature and Germination
sections.content: A temperature of 25-27 C encourages rapid germination, initial growth and flower formation.

sections.heading: Light Periods and Flowering
items: Sesame is a short day plant with 10-hour day length in 42-45 days for flowering.
Many varieties have become adapted to various light periods with wide yield variations.

sections.heading: Soil Requirements and Resistance
sections.content: Sesame can be grown in a variety of soil types, but sandy-loam, fertile, well-drained soils are ideal for its good growth and high yield. It is extremely susceptible to salinity and salt concentrations.

sections.heading: Rainfall Requirements and Distribution
sections.content: For high yield, rainfall should be distributed over the period of its growth approximately in the following proportions- 35% germination to first bud, 45% first bud to flowering and not more than 20% from flowering to maturity.

sections.heading: Soil pH and Topography
sections.content: Sesame prefers soils with neutral in reaction (pH 6.5-7.5), but can produce good yield on slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soils (pH 5.5-8.0). The sesame field should be at higher level as compare to the surroundings for quickly disposal excessive rainwater after or during heavy rainfall.

sections.heading: Cultivation and Season
sections.content: Sesame is cultivated both as a pure crop and a mixed crop with groundnut, cotton, tobacco, pigeon pea, jower, mung etc in kharif season. It is also grown as pure crop during both kharif and pre-kharif season.

title: Crop Varieties (State Wise)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Most crop varieties take 80-95 days to mature during all the seasons, with productivity varying from 350-400 kg/ha in kharif, 600-800 kg/ha in rabi, and 800-1000 kg/ha in pre-kharif.

sections.heading: Land Preparation
sections.content: Soil should be pulverized well. About 2-3 crosswise ploughing is required for sowing the crop in sandy loam type of loose soils and 3-4 ploughing are needed to make fine tilth of the silty loam field.

sections.heading: Season and Sowing
sections.content: Sesame is mainly a kharif season crop. This crop is usually sown early in the season as compare to other kharif crops. Time of sowing depends on the onset of monsoon in kharif season.

title: Sowing Time of Sesame in Different Regions in India
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: The sowing time of sesame varies across different regions in India, depending on the kharif season.

sections.heading: Sesame Sowing Time by Region
sections.content: Sesame is sown at different times in various regions of India. In southern India, it is sown during the kharif season, starting from 2nd half of May. In eastern and central India, it is sown as a rainfed crop during the same period. In northern India, it is sown towards the end of July.

sections.heading: Pre-Kharif Crop
sections.content: Sesame can also be grown as a pre-kharif crop in different regions of India. This type of crop is generally sown from the end of February to 1st half of March in central and eastern India.

title: Sowing Methods for Sesame Seeds
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Sesame seeds are sown at temperatures above 20 C, with alternative crops grown in south India where temperature fluctuations are minimal.

sections.heading: Method of Sowing
sections.content: In mixed cropping, the seed is sown either in parallel rows alternating with the main crop or broadcast in the entire field. In pure cropping, it is generally broad cast.

sections.heading: Seed Treatment
sections.content: Sesame seeds must be treated with fungicides like Agrosan G N, Tafason, Aratan 6, Mancozeb 75% WP, Carbendazin 50% WP, Dithane M-45 or Indofil-4-45 to protect them from infection.

sections.heading: Spacing
sections.content: During kharif, 35-40 cm row to row and 15-20 cm plant to plant spacing is recommended. During pre-kharif season, 30 cm row to row X 10 cm plant to plant spacing is followed.

sections.heading: Depth of Sowing
sections.content: 2.0-2.5 cm depth of sowing was the best for sesame seeds. Both shallow and deep sowing should be avoided for better emergence and uniform crop stand.

sections.heading: Manuring
sections.content: FYM 5-7 t/ha should be applied 10-15 days before sowing, mixed thoroughly with soil during ploughing. Additional fertilizers may be applied for irrigated kharif crop.

title: Intercultural Operation
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Thinning and weeding are the most important cultural operations done in sesame cultivation.

sections.heading: Thinning
sections.content: Thinning and weeding are the most important cultural operations done in sesame cultivation. If the seeds germinate properly about 80-100 plants/m appear in the field. These excess plants must be removed from the field to facilitate good growth necessary for obtaining high crop yield. Huge number of plants has to be thinned out to maintain optimum plant density.

sections.heading: First Thinning
sections.content: The first thinning is generally done at 10-15 DAS when the weak and abnormal plants are uprooted leaving the healthy plants in the field. At this stage, 10-15% more plants are kept so that if some plants die the extra plants cover up the gap.

sections.heading: Final Thinning
sections.content: The final thinning is done 10 days after the first thinning when the extra plants if present at close distance are removed to maintain optimum plant density. During this stage, weeding has also been done.

sections.heading: Weeding
sections.content: To get good harvest, the crop should be kept free of weeds at early stages of growth. Several weeds are infested the sesame field particularly during kharif season and causes considerably yield loss.

sections.heading: Control of Weeds
sections.content: Normally the weeds are controlled by hand weeding. One hand weeding at 10-15 DAS and another at 25-30 DAS can control the weeds very effectively and keep the sesame field clean and produce good yield of kharif crop.

sections.heading: Application of Alachlor
sections.content: The application of alachlor 1.5 kg/ha at 1 DAS in 500 liters of water effectively controlled weeds in sesame field and recorded quite high yield comparable to that of weed free check.

sections.heading: Irrigation
sections.content: Kharif sesame is generally grown under rainfed condition in India. However, if dry spell occurs coinciding with flowering or capsule setting, one irrigation under such condition can provide 10-15% more yield.

sections.heading: Water Requirement for Irrigation
sections.content: Pre-kharif crop requires irrigation due to scarcity of rain water. Here, irrigation must be given at critical growth stages like seedling (10-15 DAS), branching (25-30 DAS), peak flowering (45-50 DAS) and capsule development (65- 70 DAS) stages.

title: Sesame Field Management
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Controlled by spraying Chlorpyriphos 2.5 ml/l, Dimecron 40 EC 1.5 ml/l at initial stage of infestation to prevent diseases such as leaf spot, stem rot, charcoal rot, root rot, and blight.

sections.heading: Diseases
sections.content: Leaf spot (Cercospora sesami), stem rot (Macrophoma sesami), charcoal rot (Macrophomina phaseolina), root rot (Thielaviopsis basicola) and blight (Phytophthora nicotiana var sesami) are important diseases that should be prevented by following suitable crop rotation, seed treatment, using disease-free good quality seeds.

sections.heading: Phyllody and Leaf-Hoppers
sections.content: Phyllody is the most destructive disease of sesame caused by mycoplasma like organism transmitted through leaf-hoppers. The attack of leaf-hoppers should be controlled by spraying insecticide.

sections.heading: Harvesting
sections.content: Sesame is normally takes 80-95 days to mature. Harvesting should be done early morning hours of the day at a relatively low temperature and high humidity to avoid shattering of seeds.

sections.heading: Harvesting Procedure
sections.content: The plants should be cut before all capsules are mature to avoid loss of seed yield due to shattering. Immediately after harvesting, the crop should be brought to the threshing floor and stacked in the floor for 2 days then spread over the floor in sun for drying and threshing.

sections.heading: Threshing
sections.content: Threshing is done by beating the upper parts of plants with sticks or by run over of animals. Immediately after threshing the seeds should be cleaned and dried again to reduce moisture content to around 7% for storing or marketing.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.content: 8-10 q of seeds per ha

title: Use of Sesame Seed
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: 77.7% of sesame seeds are used for oil extraction, while 20% are used for domestic purposes, and 2.3% are used for seed purpose.

sections.heading: Domestic Use
sections.content: Sesame seeds are used either normal or fried for the preparation of various types of foodstuffs, sweets, cakes, pastry etc. It is also used in most of the family functions. Parched seeds are sprinkled on a variety of dishes and served on ceremonial occasions.

sections.heading: Use of Oil
sections.content: Sesame oil is used as edible vegetative fat, fixative in perfumery, and scented hair oil. Low quality oil is used for lubrication, lightning purpose, and preparation of soap, resin, and paints.

title: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Sorghum is most important fodder crop for livestock because of its wide adaptation, rapid growth, high green and dry fodder, ratoon ability and drought tolerance.

sections.heading: Uses of Sorghum
sections.content: Besides being an important food crop, sorghum is also valued for its fodder and stover. Sorghum fodder is suitable silage and hay making and thus can supplement the fodder supply during lean season.

sections.heading: Advantages of Sorghum
items: Suitable for cultivation in areas that are too dry for maize.
Dry stover forms important feeding stock for animals especially in dry areas.
Livestock relishes its fodder due to sucrose content in its straw.

title: Origin and History of Sorghum
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Cultivated sorghum probably originated in East Central Africa, in or near Ethiopia or sudan because of the great diversity of types growing in that region.

sections.heading: Types of Sorghum
sections.content: It is known under a great many names: milo, guinea corn in West Africa, kafir corn in South Africa, durra in Sudan, mtama in eastern Africa, jowar in India and kaoliang in China.

title: Soil and its preparation
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Well drained sandy loam to loam soils with a pH range of 6.5 to 7.5 are ideally suited for its cultivation.

sections.heading: Preparation of Soil
sections.content: The field should be thoroughly prepared and levelled to make weeds free sowing. Better crop stand is obtained on well-prepared soils.

sections.heading: Soil Preparation Steps

sections.heading: Importance of Drainage

sections.content: Dual purpose varieties/hybrids are resistant to leaf diseases and drought. They yield about 45-50 t/ha of green fodder.

title: Fertilizer Requirement
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The amount of fertilizer required to meet the needs of crops for secondary and micro nutrients.

sections.heading: General Guidelines
sections.content: In single cut varieties, basal application of 60:30:30 Kg N: P2O5: K2O per hectare should be given at sowing time followed by top dressing with 30 Kg N/ha, one month after sowing.

sections.heading: Adjustments for Climate and Soil Conditions
items: In low rainfall and rainfed areas, 60 Kg N/ha is applied at sowing time.
For two cuts and multicut, dose of 60:60:60 Kg& 70:30:30 kg N: P2O5; K2O/ha, respectively, as basal should be applied.

sections.heading: Top Dressing
sections.content: Top dressing of 50 kg N/ha should be done after each cut.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.content: If crop suffers due to dry spell, spraying of 2 % urea solution should be done. In sulphur deficient soils (below 10 ppm available S), the application of 40-60 Kg S/ha is advantageous not only for improving biomass production but quality f the fodder also.

sections.heading: Cutting Height for Multi Cut Varieties
sections.content: In multi cut varieties, first cut should be taken 8-10 cm above ground level so as to facilitate profuse tillering.

category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech

sections.heading: Causes and Effects of HCN
sections.content: Heavy nitrogen fertilization and water stress increases HCN content. Silage or hay making removes the toxin.

sections.heading: Harvesting and Handling
items: Irrigation before harvest may be effective in reducing HCN.
For hay making, pre-flowering is ideal stage for harvest.

sections.heading: Maturity and Risk of Poisoning

sections.content: Seed rate and sowing method are crucial factors in determining the yield of a crop. The ideal seed rate and sowing method vary depending on the crop variety, region, and weather conditions.

definition: The management of nutrients in agriculture to optimize crop growth and minimize environmental impact.

sections.heading: Varieties and Areas of Cultivation
sections.content: Different varieties of crops have varying nutrient requirements, which can be met by adjusting the amount of fertilizer applied based on factors such as region, soil type, and climate.

title: Diseases and Insect Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Diseases and Insect management
definition: Management of diseases and insect pests in agriculture.

sections.heading: Mosaic Virus Disease
sections.content: It is a serious seed-borne disease of cowpea. The symptoms appear as chlorotic patches on cotyledons, that later cover entire foliage. The secondary infection spreads through aphids. Selection resistant varieties, use of healthy seeds, control of aphids and rouging of infected plants are useful in its management.

sections.heading: Jassids (Empoascakerri)
sections.content: Both nymphs and adults suck sap from leaves in dry weather. Affected leaves turn yellow and fall off. Spray 0.03% Monocrotofos or Phosphamidon is effective.

sections.heading: Flea/Galerucid Beetle (Madurasia obscurella)
sections.content: The beetle feeds on leaves, buds and flowers. Severe attack can cause defoliation. Apply phorate 10 G kg/ha at sowing along with early sowing to avoid pest attack.

sections.heading: Hairy Caterpillar (Amsactamoorei)
sections.content: The young larvae feed on lower surface of leaves and skeletonize them leading to severe yield losses. Collection and destroying eggs and larvae in early stages. Dusting 0.05% dichlorovos spray is recommended.

sections.heading: Cowpea Stem Fly (Melangromyza phaseoli)
sections.content: The maggots bore into younger stems and tunnels towards the base causing damage to stem. The affected plants wither and die. Clean culture, use of resistant varieties and 0.05% monocrotophos spray control stem fly.

title: Harvesting Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The management of harvesting, including timing and conditions, to optimize crop yields.

sections.heading: Timing of Harvesting
sections.content: Rainy season crop is harvested after 55-60 days of sowing at 50 % flowering stage whereas summer crop requires few days and should be harvested after 70-75 days of sowing.

sections.heading: Yield Levels by Irrigation Condition
items: Under irrigated condition: 25-30 t/ha green biomass; Under rainfed condition: 15-20 t/ha.

title: Cluster Bean or Guar (Cyamopsis tetragonaloba L)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Clusterbean is a multipurpose legume of papilionaceae family valued for its gum, seed, and fodder production besides green manuring.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Uses
sections.content: The fodder of clusterbean as well as its grain is quite nutritive, rich in protein, fat and minerals. The crude protein and crude fibre content varies from 15-18% and 25-30%, respectively.

sections.heading: Cultivation and Production
sections.content: It can be grown alone or mixed with sorghum, Bajra, etc. Its gum is highly mucilaginous, which is being used in various industries such as textiles, cosmetics, explosives, paper, food processing etc.

sections.heading: Economic Importance
sections.content: Today clusterbean is one of the significant foreign exchange earner of the country. Clusterbean is grown on about 2 lakh ha in India mainly in the states of Rajasthan, Haryana, Gujarat, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra.

title: Bacterial Blight Management
category: Technical and Production Science | Disease and Insect management
definition: Bacterial blight is a seed borne disease that appears as small water soaked lesions on leaves, which later become necrotic, and may also appear on flowers and pods.

sections.heading: Management of Bacterial Blight
sections.content: Seed treatment with hot water at 50C for 10 minutes controls the disease. At the appearance of disease or at 8 weeks after sowing, spray the crop with 75 g streptocyclin and 500 g copperoxicloride in 500 litre of water to save the crop from this disease.

sections.heading: Alternaria Leaf Spot Management
sections.content: Spray Dithane Z 78 (0.2%) at an interval of 15 days is effective in its control.

title: Cotton (Gossypium spp L.)
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Cotton is one of the most important commercial crop, grown for fibre world over.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Cotton
sections.content: Fibre is used for making cloth, thread and other synthetic fibres. The fibre is almost pure cellulose.

sections.heading: Cotton Seed
items: contains 15-25% oil which is used for making vegetable ghee or oil.
cotton seed cake after extraction of oil is good organic manure which contains about 6% N, 3% phosphorus and 2% potash.

sections.heading: Toxicity
sections.content: Cotton has gossypol, a toxin that makes it inedible.

title: Cotton Origin and History
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
definition: Cotton has been used as a fabric in India from time immemorial.

sections.heading: Early History of Cotton
sections.content: The excavations of Mohen-jo-daro indicates a high degree of art in spinning and weaving with cotton at that time. It finds mention in the Rig-Veda, the oldest scripture of the Hindus.

sections.heading: Native Regions of Cotton Varieties
rows: Upland cotton, native to Central America, Mexico, the Caribbean and southern Florida
Extra-long staple cotton, native to tropical South America
Tree cotton, native to India and Pakistan
Levant cotton, native to southern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula

title: Area and Distribution
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: The important cotton growing countries are India, USA, former USSR, China, Brazil, Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey, Mexico and Sudan.

sections.heading: Leading Cotton-Producing States in India
sections.content: In India, the states of Maharashtra (26.63%), Gujarat (17.96%) and Andhra Pradesh (13.75%) are the leading cotton producing states, these states have a predominantly tropical wet and dry climate.

sections.heading: Global Cotton Production
items: The five leading exporters of cotton in 2011 are the United States, India, Brazil, Australia, and Uzbekistan.
Current estimates for world production are about 25 million tonnes annually, accounting for 2.5% of the world's arable land.

sections.heading: Global Cotton Trade
rows: China is the world's largest producer of cotton, but most of this is used domestically.
The United States has been the largest exporter for many years.

title: Cotton Crop in India
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The cotton crop is entirely dependent on rainfall in nearly 65% of the area, with supplementary irrigation facilities available in 35% of the area.

sections.heading: Maximum Productivity by State
sections.content: Gujarat state has the maximum productivity of 774 kg/ha, followed by Andhra Pradesh at 748 kg/ha, with a national average of 591 kg/ha.

sections.heading: Haryana State Data (2009-10)
sections.content: The area, production and productivity of Haryana state were 5.07 lakh ha, 19.3 lakh bales each of 170 kg and 650 kg/ha, respectively.
